latin.557: Imputant nonnunquam homines vel ignari, vel iniusti, aliis hominibus peccata, qui non peccarunt; & qui peccarunt, his nonnunquam Deus peccata non imputat: Et, si cui Deus peccatum imputat, imputat quia peccavit, non facit imputando ut peccaverit. Ordine naturae prius peccatur, quam peccatum imputatur.
latin.558: GAR. Resp. 3. Deus nemini peccatum imputat, quin ille peccaverit vel in se, vel in alio, id est, quin vel in se peccatum commiserit, vel alius, quocum arcte coniunctus est; sicut Sauli peccatum filiis eius imputavit, non quia ipsi commisissent, sed quia pater eorum commiserat. Et item Deus testatur in lege, se visitare peccata patrum in filiis.
latin.559: Deus imputando peccatum alicui, non facit ut peccaverit, sed supponit eum peccavisse, sive in se, sive in alio. Est enim imputatio peccati actus Dei iudicialis, quo declarat aliquem esse reum & dignum poena ob peccatum, ut ab initio dictum.
latin.560: Peccatur prius ab aliquo, quam peccatum imputetur; sed non est necessarium, ut ab eo ipso cui peccatum imputatur, prius actu peccatum fuerit; sed necessarium est, ut aliquam habeat coniunctionem cum eo qui peccavit, & cuius peccatum ei imputatur, sicut antea docuit Clar. Amyraldus.
latin.561: PLAC. Idem sonare mihi videntur tres istae Viri docti responsiones; simul igitur omnes refellam. Principio distinguenda est coniunctio cum peccatore: alia enim est coniunctio cum peccatore quatenus est peccator, alia cum peccatore quatenus est homo a quo ducimus originem. Vacare peccato non potest qui cum peccatore coniunctus est quatenus est peccator: particeps enim est eiusdem peccati, vel consensione, vel propagatione, vel imitatione &c.
latin.562: At coniunctio cum alio, quatenus homo est a quo ducimus originem, sola non sufficit, ut peccatum ab alio commissum imputetur: alioqui omnia Adami, omniaque parentum nostrorum peccata, nobis possent iure imputari, quod, opinor, nemo dixerit: nulla tamen alia coniunctio nos inter & Adamum, ante communicatam ab eo corruptionem haereditariam, esse potuit. Nec iuvat Virum doctum exemplum Saulis: Nam eius filii, cum in se peccatores erant ac digni ob propria peccata illis poenis quas perpessi sunt, tum peccati illius paterni participes, ut patet ex verbis ipsius Dei 2. Sam. 21. 1. Propter Saulem, & domum eius sanguinariam, eo quod interfecit Gibeonitas. Non igitur solus Saul erat sanguinarius, sed eius domus seu familia.

pass_a.557: Placeus first: false human imputation can land on the innocent, and God may withhold imputation from the guilty. When God does impute, he does so because the person sinned—he does not create the sin by the verdict. Nature's order puts the act before the imputation.
pass_a.558: GAR's third reply: God never imputes unless the person sinned in himself or in another tightly joined to him—as Saul's sin was laid on his sons, and as the law visits fathers' sins on children.
pass_a.559: Imputation does not make someone to have sinned; it presupposes that he sinned, in himself or in another. It is God's judicial act declaring him guilty and penalty-worthy for sin.
pass_a.560: Someone sins before sin is imputed. The one charged need not have done the act himself first, but must be joined to the one who did—Amyraut's point already taught.
pass_a.561: Placeus treats the learned man's three answers as one voice and refutes them together. First split the bond with the sinner: joined to him insofar as he is a sinner—by consent, propagation, or imitation—you cannot be free of that same sin. Joined to him only insofar as he is the man from whom you draw origin is a different bond and must not be confused with the first.
pass_a.562: Mere descent from Adam, without the hereditary corruption he shared, cannot ground imputation of another's act—or else every sin of Adam and of our parents could be charged to us, which no one allows. Before that corruption there was no other bond with Adam. Saul's sons already stood sinners in themselves and sharers in the bloody house (2 Sam 21:1), so the example does not prove bare origin. Tip before Placeus turns the contradiction.

557: Men, whether ignorant or unjust, sometimes impute to other men sins who have not sinned; and to those who have sinned God sometimes does not impute sins: And, if to anyone God imputes sin, he imputes because he has sinned; he does not by imputing make him to have sinned. In the order of nature it is first sinned, before sin is imputed.
558: GAR. Answer 3. God imputes sin to no one unless he has sinned either in himself, or in another, that is, unless either he has committed sin in himself, or another with whom he is closely joined; as he imputed Saul's sin to his sons, not because they themselves had committed it, but because their father had committed it. And likewise God testifies in the law that he visits the sins of the fathers upon the children.
559: God, by imputing sin to someone, does not make him to have sinned, but supposes him to have sinned, whether in himself or in another. For the imputation of sin is a judicial act of God, by which he declares someone to be guilty and worthy of penalty on account of sin, as was said from the beginning.
560: It is sinned first by someone, before sin is imputed; but it is not necessary that by that very one to whom sin is imputed, sin should first have been by act; but it is necessary that he have some conjunction with him who sinned, and whose sin is imputed to him, as the learned Amyraut taught before.
561: PLAC. Those three replies of the learned man seem to me to sound the same; I will therefore refute them all together. First the conjunction with the sinner must be distinguished: for one is conjunction with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner, another with the sinner insofar as he is the man from whom we draw our origin. He cannot be free from sin who is joined with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner: for he is a partaker of the same sin, whether by consent, or by propagation, or by imitation, and so on.
562: But conjunction with another, insofar as he is the man from whom we draw origin, alone does not suffice for a sin committed by another to be imputed: otherwise all Adam's sins, and all our parents' sins, could rightly be imputed to us, which, I think, no one would say: yet no other conjunction between us and Adam could have existed before the hereditary corruption communicated by him. Nor does the example of Saul help the learned man: For his sons, when they were sinners in themselves and worthy on account of their own sins of those penalties which they suffered, were then also partakers of that paternal sin, as is clear from the words of God himself, 2 Samuel 21. 1. For Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Therefore not Saul alone was bloody, but his house or family.
